units.title: On-policy generation and the sequence policy gradient
outcomes: Derive the sequence policy gradient from the autoregressive factorization with a fixed prompt distribution.
Identify the distribution that actually generated a completion and the log probabilities its update requires.
units.why: The sequence objective is familiar REINFORCE, but generation now owns the sampling distribution. A correct loss on text drawn from a different decoding policy is not an on-policy estimator.

next.note: Turn the sequence derivative into a masked token loss.

study.title: RLHF Book: sequence policy gradient
study.locator: Chapter 6, The Role of Reinforcement Learning in RLHF and Deriving the Policy Gradient, equations 9 to 18 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 3: RL Motivation and Math
study.locator: Slides 20 to 28: differentiating the expectation, trajectory factorization and the token-log-probability sum
study.depth: Build on the earlier likelihood-ratio identity and Decoding policies: from greedy to nucleus sampling. Skip the classical RL review before slide 20.

focus: For a fixed prompt distribution and parameter-independent reward, \(\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb{E}[R(x,y)\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})]\). Include the sampled stopping action when EOS ends the response.
The prompt distribution and deterministic append transition have zero parameter derivative. The completion distribution does not.
Temperature and truncation change the policy, not just its presentation. Start with untruncated categorical sampling at temperature 1; otherwise define and score the transformed policy explicitly.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, enumerate a two-token binary policy with independent tokens, each with probability \(p\) of 1, and reward 1 only for two ones. Derive \(J(p)=p^2\) and recover \(dJ/dp=2p\) from the expected score-function estimator. At \(p=1/2\), both give 1. This oracle needs only CPU arithmetic.
traps: Backpropagating the mean of frozen verifier scores. It has no path to policy parameters; the score-function loss supplies that path.
Calling a completion on-policy because its model weights match. Top-p filtering, temperature, dropout and numerical backend differences can still change its distribution.

selfTest.q: Why is there no explicit trajectory probability multiplying each sampled gradient?
selfTest.a: Sampling already weights trajectories by their probability. Multiplying by that probability again estimates a different expectation.

selfTest.q: Does the sequence gradient require gradients through sampled token IDs?
selfTest.a: No. Hold the sampled IDs fixed and differentiate their log probabilities under the policy.

selfTest.q: Can raw model log probabilities describe nucleus sampling exactly?
selfTest.a: No. The sampler removes tokens and renormalizes the retained probabilities. Raw log probabilities omit that transformation and its support restriction.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the sequence-gradient oracle and the generation-policy contract in policylab's rollout collector.
units.stopWhen: Your enumeration matches the analytic derivative for several probabilities, and you can name the sampler and scoring distribution for every rollout.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 3 supply the derivation; the mini-project supplies an exact finite-policy oracle and sampling-contract practice.

units.title: Terminal rewards, per-token loss assignment and token-space REINFORCE
outcomes: Derive why an undiscounted terminal reward weights every generated token in REINFORCE.
Implement a completion-summed loss with detached rewards and test its token gradients.
units.why: A terminal score must reach the whole completion, not just its last token. The loss reduction decides whether you optimize expected sequence reward or a length-reweighted surrogate.

next.note: Replace the broadcast return with prefix-dependent advantages.

study.title: RLHF Book: REINFORCE in token space
study.locator: Chapter 6, REINFORCE, then Implementation: Policy-Gradient Basics and Related: MDP vs. Bandit Framing (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Lecture 4: summed token log probabilities
study.locator: Slides 8 to 12: log-probability shift, gather, completion sum and REINFORCE loss
study.depth: Use a fixed or previously fitted baseline first. Slide 12's current-batch mean includes each sample's own reward; it is not an action-independent baseline. The RLOO unit checks that distinction.

focus: With terminal reward only and \(\gamma=1\), every completion token has return \(R\). Broadcasting this return is not a claim that each token independently caused the outcome.
Use \(L=-B^{-1}\sum_i A_i\sum_t m_{i,t}\log\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x_i,y_{i,<t})\). A variable per-response token mean changes the weighting.
Build on Masks, sequence log probabilities and Log-probability oracles and prompt separation. Rewards, baselines and sampled IDs are fixed; selected current log probabilities carry gradients.
units.reproduce: On CPU, use `torch.float64` selected log probabilities `[[-1., -2., -9.], [-3., -8., -7.]]`, completion masks `[[1., 1., 0.], [1., 0., 0.]]` and detached advantages `[2., -1.]`. Sum tokens, average the two sequence losses and obtain loss 1.5. Gradients with respect to selected log probabilities are `[[-1., -1., 0.], [0.5, 0., 0.]]` within floating-point tolerance.
traps: Putting the loss only on EOS because the reward arrived there. Reward placement and gradient assignment are different operations.
Replacing the token sum with a token mean without naming the changed objective. Variable response lengths make this more than a fixed learning-rate rescaling.
Reading a lower frozen-rollout loss as better generation. Only fresh, independently scored outputs establish behavior change.

selfTest.q: Does repeating the terminal return across tokens count the reward several times?
selfTest.a: No. It weights separate terms in the derivative of the sequence log probability. Do not also repeat the terminal reward in the reward-to-go calculation.

selfTest.q: What changes if terminal reward is discounted?
selfTest.a: Returns depend on the distance to termination. Derive the discounted objective and its score-function weights explicitly rather than broadcasting an undiscounted score.

selfTest.q: Why must changing finite padding log probabilities leave the loss unchanged?
selfTest.a: Padding is not a sampled action. The completion mask removes it from both the loss and its selected-log-probability gradient.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's terminal-reward REINFORCE loss, hand gradients and padding-invariance tests.
units.stopWhen: Your loss and selected-log-probability gradients match the fixed example, and you can explain why a variable-length token mean is a different weighting.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 4 reach derive and implement depth; the mini-project checks terminal credit and the exact reduction.

units.title: PPO-style RLHF with a value critic, and critic cost versus group sampling
outcomes: Derive prefix-value targets and token advantages for PPO-style RLHF with terminal rewards and KL shaping.
Explain the separate actor and critic losses and which rollout quantities stay fixed.
Compare critic state and fitting cost with extra group generation and verifier calls under a common budget.
units.why: A critic can exploit prefix information that a sequence baseline cannot. It also adds learned state and another failure mode; removing it trades that burden for sibling sampling, not free variance reduction.

next.note: Estimate a prompt baseline without fitting a value model.

study.title: RLHF Book: language PPO and value targets
study.locator: Chapter 6, Value Functions and PPO, Example: PPO, and Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Reuse the earlier GAE and PPO derivations. Concentrate on completion boundaries, KL-shaped returns and critic targets; use rollout-time values for actor advantages.

study.title: Lecture 4: PPO implementation and its cost
study.locator: Slides 16 to 28, 30 and 35: rollout tensors, targets, critic clipping, initialization and resident model state
study.depth: Slide 27's claim that a prediction close to the target is unaffected by value clipping is not general: the maximum can select the larger clipped error. Check both branches.

focus: The critic scores the prefix before the action, not the completed answer. Its target includes future outcome reward and future KL-shaped token rewards.
Freeze old values, returns and actor advantages during batch reuse. Keep unwhitened advantages for constructing critic targets; whitening actor weights must not alter those targets.

Build the state ledger using GPU memory: allocated, reserved, peak and memory models. A separate critic needs parameters, gradients, optimizer state and activations; a shared value head changes the ledger and couples the losses.

Compare variance on the same task and sampling budget. A critic is not guaranteed to reduce it, and group baselines require extra generated tokens and scoring calls. TRL 1.15.0 has no `PPOTrainer`; this path is a scratch estimator.
units.reproduce: For a completed three-token response, use rewards `[0., 0., 2.]`, rollout-time prefix values `[0.5, 1., 1.5]`, zero terminal bootstrap and \(\gamma=\lambda=1\). Recover advantages `[1.5, 1., 0.5]` and value targets `[2., 2., 2.]`. Then hand-check optional critic clipping with old value 0, current value 1, target 1 and clip width 0.2: the maximum of the two half-squared errors is 0.32, not zero.
traps: Using the critic's newly fitted values to recompute advantages after every minibatch. The actor's fixed surrogate then changes underneath the optimizer.
Assuming every PPO implementation holds four independent full models. A verifier can replace the reward model, backbones can be shared and frozen models can be offloaded.
Adding a separate KL loss after already shaping the reward with the same penalty. That changes the objective and may double its influence.

selfTest.q: Why can advantages differ across tokens when there is only one terminal reward?
selfTest.a: Prefix values differ, and GAE combines different TD residuals. KL shaping can also introduce intermediate token rewards.

selfTest.q: Can an inaccurate fixed baseline bias terminal-return REINFORCE?
selfTest.a: Not if it depends only on the pre-action state and its gradient is excluded. Bootstrapped targets from an inaccurate critic can introduce bias; these are different mechanisms.

selfTest.q: Does the critic predict the verifier score alone?
selfTest.a: It predicts the specified future return. With KL shaping, that includes future KL penalties as well as the outcome score.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the value-based fixed-rollout estimator, critic-target oracle and critic-versus-group cost ledger.
units.stopWhen: Your three-token advantages and targets match the oracle, both critic-clipping branches are explained, and your cost ledger includes generation as well as model state.

fit.note: Chapter 6 and Lecture 4 cover language PPO, critic targets and costs; the mini-project checks a value-based estimator without relying on a removed trainer.

units.title: Leave-one-out baselines and RLOO
outcomes: Derive the leave-one-out baseline's conditional independence and unbiased score-function estimator.
Implement prompt-grouped RLOO and distinguish it from centering by a mean that includes the current reward.
units.why: RLOO uses sibling completions as a prompt-specific baseline. Excluding the current reward is the part that preserves the expected REINFORCE gradient.

next.note: Separate group centering from standard-deviation scaling and clipping.

study.title: RLHF Book: RLOO algebra
study.locator: Chapter 6, REINFORCE Leave One Out (RLOO), equations 25 to 27 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Back to Basics: sequence REINFORCE and RLOO
study.locator: arXiv:2402.14740v2, Sections 2.2 and 2.3, printed pp. 5 to 6: sequence estimator, moving-average baseline and the unnumbered RLOO estimator
study.depth: Stop before Section 2.4. The paper's model-scale comparisons are evidence for its setup, not a guarantee that RLOO beats PPO on your task.

focus: For \(K>1\) independent completions of one prompt, \(b_i=(K-1)^{-1}\sum_{j\ne i}R_j\). Conditional on the prompt, sibling rewards do not depend on the current sampled completion.

The identity \(A_i=\frac{K}{K-1}(R_i-\bar R)\) makes the finite-sample correction explicit. Centering alone shrinks the expected raw-reward gradient by \((K-1)/K\) under the same independence assumptions.
Keep siblings grouped by prompt identity, not their position after shuffling. Treat KL-shaped rewards as fixed score-function weights; do not differentiate through the baseline.
units.reproduce: For one prompt with rewards `[0., 1., 2.]`, obtain leave-one-out baselines `[1.5, 1., 0.5]` and advantages `[-1.5, 0., 1.5]`. Enumerate all pairs of independent binary completions with success probability \(p=1/2\), reward equal to the sampled bit and score \(\partial_p\log\pi\). The expected two-sample RLOO estimate is 1; centering by the inclusive mean gives 0.5. Verify by exact enumeration on CPU, not a Monte Carlo run.
traps: Using the whole minibatch as the sibling group. Prompt difficulty then contaminates the intended per-prompt baseline.
Generating siblings by dependent selection and still invoking the independent-sample proof. Best-of-N winners and sampling without replacement need a different analysis.
Using a singleton group. Its leave-one-out denominator is zero; reject it or choose a separately specified baseline.

selfTest.q: Is detaching an inclusive batch mean enough to make it action-independent?
selfTest.a: No. Detachment removes an autodiff path, not statistical dependence on the current sampled reward.

selfTest.q: Why does the baseline term have zero expectation?
selfTest.a: Condition on the prompt and the independent siblings. Their baseline is fixed while the current completion's expected score is zero.

selfTest.q: Does RLOO need a learned value model?
selfTest.a: No. It uses extra completions and reward calls to estimate the baseline. Those calls still belong in the cost budget.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: policylab's RLOO baseline, prompt-regrouping tests and exact expected-gradient comparison.
units.stopWhen: Your leave-one-out and inclusive-mean estimates match the enumeration, and shuffling complete rollout records preserves prompt-specific advantages.

fit.note: The book's algebra and the original RLOO estimator cover the derivation; the mini-project provides independence and regrouping tests.

units.title: Grouped sampling, group-relative advantages, GRPO and degenerate groups
outcomes: Derive outcome-supervised group advantages and identify their differences from RLOO.
Implement a critic-free clipped loss that handles mixed and all-equal reward groups.
units.why: GRPO replaces a fitted critic with comparisons between sibling completions. Its useful signal depends on reward differences within a prompt, not just on average success.

next.note: Measure how the normalization changes prompt weighting.

study.title: RLHF Book: GRPO
study.locator: Chapter 6, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), equations 33 to 38 (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: DeepSeekMath: original outcome-supervised GRPO
study.locator: arXiv:2402.03300v3, Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.2, equations 3 to 5 and Figure 4
study.depth: Stop before process supervision in Section 4.1.3. Keep the original token ratios and per-response means separate from later trainer defaults.

focus: For outcome rewards, broadcast \(A_i=(R_i-\bar R)/(s_R+\delta)\) to completion tokens. Specify population or sample standard deviation, a positive stabilizer and a minimum group size.
Group centering, standard-deviation scaling, ratio clipping, KL placement and aggregation are separate choices. The algorithm name alone does not specify your loss.

All-equal rewards give zero outcome advantages with a finite denominator. All-correct and all-wrong binary groups share that property, but require different data decisions. An explicit KL term can still supply gradients.
The original method removes the critic and GAE. It does not remove sibling generation, verification or the need to test loss gradients.
units.reproduce: On CPU, normalize rewards `[1., 1., 0., 0.]` with population standard deviation and stabilizer `1e-4`. Obtain advantages approximately `[0.99980004, 0.99980004, -0.99980004, -0.99980004]`. Repeat with sample standard deviation: magnitudes become approximately 0.86587543. All-zero and all-one groups must give finite zero advantages. Reject a singleton before computing a sample standard deviation.
traps: Treating normalized inclusive centering as the unbiased RLOO estimator. The random denominator adds another dependence on the sampled group.
Adding a stabilizer after division. It cannot repair a zero denominator or an already undefined singleton sample standard deviation.
Calling all-correct groups proof of generalization. The held-out prompt distribution may still fail.

selfTest.q: Does zero mean advantage imply zero policy gradient?
selfTest.a: No. Different completions have different score vectors. Their weighted gradients need not cancel.

selfTest.q: Does an all-wrong binary group identify the least wrong completion?
selfTest.a: No. Equal verifier rewards give no relative outcome information. Use a specified richer reward or change sampling, not an invented ranking.

selfTest.q: Why do NumPy and PyTorch ports sometimes disagree?
selfTest.a: Their default standard-deviation corrections differ. Specify the convention and stabilizer in both implementations.

practice.name: Normalize GRPO Group Advantages
practice.locator: Language Modeling from Scratch plan, Normalize GRPO Group Advantages: statement, function signature and public examples
practice.note: The problem uses population standard deviation. The section mini-project also tests sample-standard-deviation parity and degenerate groups.

units.stopWhen: Your mixed and all-equal groups match the specified convention, and you can list every choice needed to turn those advantages into a loss.
